Long story short: until Bethesda stops breaking the modding communities' collective souls, it is best to steer clear of SSE mods. However, of the base game much positive can be said. [i]The Elder Scrolls[/i] is an odd series, encompassing a massive span of time and an impressive amount of technological, game design, and gameplay innovation. Its fifth installment, [i]Skyrim[/i], is a particularly odd entry in the series, representing a further shift in focus, rather than emphasizing role-playing, shifting to the action in ARPG. Its predecessor, [i]Oblivion[/i], made a substantial leap in this direction already, but [i]Skyrim[/i] fully commits to this fundamental change, even bringing in heavy contemporary influence from the film adaptations of Tolkien's [i]Lord of the Rings[/i]. It is hardly the only franchise to embrace this aesthetic shift, but its popularity makes the change impossible to ignore and perhaps, theoretically, culturally terminal within video games. The influence of the series shifts from the films to [i]Skyrim[/i] itself, creating a new focal point for comparison within the gaming industry. [i]Skyrim[/i] also created and improved on several landmarks for ARPG roleplaying elements, such as the use-based skill system, massively increased map size (without sacrificing interaction), and, perhaps most importantly, ideal modding infrastructure which substantially lengthened the game's lifespan and relevance. While it was plagued with bugs and instability on release, the state of the game has changed drastically over time, particularly with [i]Skyrim Special Edition[/i] and [i]Skyrim Anniversary Edition[/i]. While the sale of [i]Special Edition[/i] was perhaps necessary to make the game more accessible and stable, the [i]Anniversary Edition[/i] is largely unnecessary and exists as a cash-grab more than a value-add release. Bethesda now fully realizes and recognizes the success of the installment, resting on its laurels for decades past its release, particularly with additional releases, but additionally with the lack of urgency in sequel production.

The base game offers more than enough content to enjoy - for hundreds (or even thousands) of hours - but the addition of DLC ([i]Hearthfire[/i], [i]Dawnguard[/i], and [i]Dragonborn[/i]) add many more opportunities for additional story and immersion. [i]Hearthfire[/i] particularly capitalizes on many players' immersive interest in homesteading gameplay, paralleling the then re-emerging simulation genre. The [i]Dawnguard[/i] and [i]Dragonborn[/i] DLCs offer better stories than [i]Skyrim[/i]'s main quest line, but perhaps not equal to the more interesting side quests from the main game. This is where [i]Skyrim[/i], and every [i]Elder Scrolls[/i] installment since [i]Daggerfall[/i] ([i]Elder Scrolls II[/i]), stands out: in the unscheduled, unprompted, happenstance side quests. In the “living world” format of the series, random encounters, NPCS, and landscapes can be just as - or likely more - exciting than scripted scenes or quests. This is just as true for the role-playing systems that support the gameplay, like smithing, alchemy, or the schools of magic, where the interplay of skill-based leveling brings meaning to all tasks and encounters, not just those driven by story progression (true of any worthwhile role-playing experience). The role-playing action is where [i]Skyrim[/i] separates itself from its contemporaries, and predecessors, however. The convergence of these systems with fluid combat, designed to intentionally guide players through well-paced dungeons or well-crafted environments (small worlds), creates the satisfying tension/payoff that the game is famous for. 

This is exemplified by one of the game’s high points in “Blackreach”, a sprawling underworld that bridges many of the game’s ongoing stories and quests in a satisfyingly unique ecosystem. While the gameplay does not have the depth of RPGs from other subgenres or older iterations, it has impressive breadth, and its innovation in the action genre is unmistakable, marking a turning point for ARPGS that would be felt for many years. All of these strengths are only amplified by the modding community. Players have morphed Skyrim into an altogether new product, offering a fully customizable experience that can vary wildly from player to player, and now with the implementation of tools like [i]Wabbajack[/i], a program that allows players to install preformed mod packs, the ease of modding makes these incredible experiences more realistic and practical than ever. Still, the “out of the box” iteration of [i]Skyrim[/i] (including the many subsequent re-releases) is very different from the modern mod-heavy reality that players now experience, and while it is more than worthy of exploring, it has evolved to become an entirely new game many years later.

The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim is arguably the greatest role-playing game I have ever played. Were it not for Oblivion, I would have no hesitation in making that claim. Even so, Skyrim remains a timeless masterpiece that continues to set the standard for open-world RPGs.

From its engaging leveling system and memorable quests to its breathtaking landscapes and immense sense of exploration, nearly every aspect of the game contributes to an unforgettable experience. Its world feels remarkably immersive, rewarding curiosity and making even the simplest journey feel like an adventure.

Of course, the game is not without its flaws. Bugs are an unavoidable part of the experience, although their frequency can vary. Fortunately, they rarely detract from the overall enjoyment, and many eventually become an endearing part of the game's identity.

I would strongly recommend avoiding excessive reliance on fast travel. Take the time to explore Skyrim on foot and appreciate its landscapes; some of the most memorable moments come from the unexpected encounters and discoveries along the way.

Combat preparation is equally important. Prioritize developing your combat skills early, as enemies scale with you and can quickly overwhelm an unprepared character. A balanced and well-developed build will make the progression considerably more enjoyable.

For achievement hunters, Skyrim offers a relatively accessible completion experience. Most achievements can be obtained within approximately 100 hours on your first playthrough. However, the Legendary Dragon achievement requires level 78, which can become a tedious grind without some strategic exploitation of the leveling system.

Ultimately, Skyrim is an extraordinary achievement in open-world game design. Its atmosphere, freedom, exploration, and sheer scale make it an experience that remains captivating long after its release.

Rating: 9/10 — Remarkable.

🐉 Skyrim Is Not a Game, It’s a Permanent Lifestyle 🏔️⚔️
🎮 THE GAMEPLAY

There are games you play, and then there is Skyrim. 🐉 From the moment you gain control, you're dropped into a gigantic fantasy sandbox and told to have fun. 🗺️ Fight ⚔️, sneak 🥷, explore 🏔️, craft 🔨, enchant ✨, brew potions 🧪, cast spells 🔮, hunt 🦌, fish 🎣, farm 🌾, build 🏠, ride horses 🐎 or simply wander around for hours.

The greatest thing about Skyrim is the freedom. You can start doing one thing, get distracted by something else and suddenly realize three hours have disappeared. ⏰

⚔️ COMBAT

The variety of combat is fantastic. Swords ⚔️, axes 🪓, maces 🔨, daggers 🗡️, greatswords, bows 🏹, crossbows, shields 🛡️, staves, spells 🔥❄️⚡ and Shouts 🗣️ all give you different ways to fight.

Charge into battle in heavy armor, dual-wield weapons, become a stealth archer, assassinate enemies, summon creatures 👹, burn enemies, freeze them or destroy them with lightning.

And then there is FUS RO DAH. 🐉

Launching an enemy across a room by screaming at them never gets old.

🌳 SKILLS & BUILDS

Skyrim's skill system makes progression feel natural. Use swords and One-Handed improves, use bows and Archery improves, sneak and Sneak improves, cast spells and magic improves, craft equipment and Smithing improves, make potions and Alchemy improves. 🧪

The perk trees let you specialize into warriors 🛡️, assassins 🥷, archers 🏹, mages 🔮, necromancers 💀, thieves 💰, vampires 🧛, werewolves 🐺 or ridiculous combinations of everything.

Every character can become something completely different.

🥷 STEALTH

Stealth is ridiculously satisfying. Sneak through dungeons, use bows 🏹, assassinate enemies with daggers 🗡️, use poisons ☠️ or manipulate enemies with Illusion magic.

Eventually every Skyrim player discovers the legendary build:

THE STEALTH ARCHER. 🏹🥷

You crouch, shoot someone and see Sneak increased. Suddenly you're 50 hours into a character you never intended to create.

🔮 MAGIC

Magic gives Skyrim another entire layer of gameplay. Destruction 🔥❄️⚡ provides offensive spells, Restoration ❤️ keeps you alive, Conjuration 👹 summons creatures, Alteration 🪄 provides protection and Illusion 🧠 lets you manipulate enemies.

You can heal yourself, become invisible, summon an army, raise the dead 💀 or turn an ordinary fight into complete magical chaos.

🔨 CRAFTING

Smithing 🔨, Enchanting ✨ and Alchemy 🧪 are practically games of their own.

Collect ore ⛏️, ingredients 🌿 and soul gems 💎, craft equipment, improve it, enchant it and brew potions until your character becomes an absurdly powerful monster.

You start with basic iron gear and eventually create legendary equipment specifically designed to destroy dragons. 🐉

🗺️ EXPLORATION

Exploration is one of Skyrim's greatest strengths. Caves 🕳️, mines ⛏️, forts 🏰, ruins, tombs 💀, camps and hidden locations are everywhere.

You see something interesting in the distance 👀, investigate it and suddenly you're exploring a dungeon you never knew existed.

See a mountain? 🏔️ Climb it. See a ruin? 🏛️ Explore it. See a dragon? 🐉 KILL IT.

Skyrim constantly rewards curiosity.

💎 LOOT & DUNGEONS

Nordic tombs, Dwemer ruins, caves, mines, forts, bandit camps and vampire lairs keep exploration interesting.

You're constantly fighting ⚔️, searching 🔎, solving puzzles 🧩, opening chests and finding weapons, armor, jewelry, gems 💎, ingredients, potions 🧪, scrolls 📜 and unique artifacts.

The only real problem is inventory space.

You enter carrying nothing and leave carrying 14 swords, several helmets, a mountain of Dwemer scrap and enough cheese 🧀 to feed an army.

Naturally, you pick up more.

🌎 THE SANDBOX

You don't even need to complete quests. Hunt 🦌, mine ⛏️, chop wood 🪵, cook 🍖, fish 🎣, farm 🌾, craft 🔨, enchant ✨, build 🏠, ride horses 🐎, read books 📚 or simply explore.

Skyrim gives you freedom without constantly telling you what to do.

🎣 ANNIVERSARY EDITION

Anniversary Edition adds even more gameplay through Fishing 🎣, Survival Mode 🥶, Farming 🌾, Saints & Seducers 😈, Rare Curios 🧪, new weapons ⚔️, armor 🛡️, spells 🔮, enemies 👹, homes 🏠 and quests 📜.

Ghosts of the Tribunal adds Morrowind-inspired equipment, The Cause adds another adventure, Forgotten Seasons provides a huge Dwemer experience and Necromantic Grimoire expands magical gameplay.

It is an already massive game with even more things to do.

🏠 HOMES & SURVIVAL

Building and decorating homes is surprisingly addictive. Bedrooms 🛏️, libraries 📚, kitchens 🍳, greenhouses 🌱, armories ⚔️ and display rooms let you create your own personal headquarters.

Survival Mode 🥶 changes the experience by making food 🍖, sleep 💤, warmth 🔥 and preparation important.

The Dragonborn can defeat dragons but apparently still struggles with being cold.

⚔️ EQUIPMENT & ENEMIES

The equipment variety is enormous. Swords ⚔️, axes 🪓, maces 🔨, daggers 🗡️, bows 🏹, shields 🛡️, staves and countless armor sets allow huge amounts of customization.

Then you have bandits, Draugr 💀, Falmer 🕷️, vampires 🧛, dragons 🐉, trolls, giants, mammoths, wolves, bears, sabre cats, Spriggans, Daedra and Dwemer machines.

There is always something waiting to kill you.

🎵 SOUND & ATMOSPHERE

The sound design is incredible. Wind 🌬️, snow ❄️, weapons ⚔️, spells 🔮 and dragon roars 🐉 make the world feel alive.

Then the music starts. 🎵

Walking through the mountains while the soundtrack kicks in is still one of gaming's great experiences.

🔁 REPLAYABILITY

Skyrim's replayability is ridiculous.

You finish one character and think, "What if I play a mage?" 🧙

Then you make a warrior ⚔️, assassin 🥷, archer 🏹 or necromancer 💀.

Then you install mods 🛠️.

Then you start again.

Different builds, equipment and playstyles can completely change the experience.

🛠️ MODS

And then there are mods.

Graphics 🎨, quests 📜, weapons ⚔️, armor 🛡️, followers 👥, locations 🗺️, spells 🔮, enemies 👹, combat systems, weather 🌧️ and animations can transform Skyrim into something completely different.

The community has essentially turned Skyrim into an endless playground.

🐛 THE BUGS

Yes, Skyrim has bugs.

Horses climb mountains 🐎🏔️, giants launch you into orbit 🚀, mammoths fly 🦣, NPCs walk into walls and dragons get stuck in buildings. 🐉

At this point they're not bugs.

They're Skyrim features.

🏆 FINAL VERDICT

Skyrim Anniversary Edition is one of the most replayable games ever created.

Combat ⚔️ offers countless approaches, skills 🌳 and perks 🔥 allow endless builds, crafting 🔨 gives you reasons to collect everything, Enchanting ✨ and Alchemy 🧪 let you create ridiculous gear, Stealth 🥷 changes how you approach combat, Magic 🔮 provides completely different playstyles and Exploration 🗺️ constantly rewards curiosity.

Add fishing 🎣, farming 🌾, Survival Mode 🥶, houses 🏠, horses 🐎, companions, hundreds of locations, countless weapons and all the Anniversary Edition content, then throw mods on top.

At that point Skyrim isn't just a game.

Its a masterpiece in open-world role-playing, a game that still feels expansive, alive, and endlessly inviting. Its atmosphere is unmatched—the haunting soundtrack, the way light filters through pine forests, the sense that every cave or Nordic ruin might hide something wondrous or deadly—and the sheer scale of its systems for crafting, magic, and character progression lets players lose hundreds of hours simply existing in Tamriel. 

The Shouts and Magic system work really well in Skyrim, and the dragon lore, combined with some very well written characters you meet along the way, complete the entire experience.

The legendary modding community transformed it into something even greater, extending its life far beyond any official support and turning it into a platform for endless creativity. I have played Skyrim for ten years and spent around 1,500 hours in the Special Edition, plus another 300 hours in the Legendary Edition. On my first playthrough, I skipped much of the dialogue and paid little attention to the main story. I knew very little about the setting, but I was already enjoying myself enormously. Whatever kept me playing was there before I had learnt much of the lore.
Looking back, I think it was the opportunity to create a character of my own, learn how the world around her worked, and decide what she would do in it. Skyrim gave me something to do with my imagination, even when I had little interest in the story it was telling.
Character customisation matters here. I prefer to play as a lady, and I appreciate being able to choose her appearance and shape her abilities rather than take on a fully prescribed role. My preferred character wears heavy armour, carries a shield and uses magic to heal and protect her companions. The combination of skills and equipment gives that idea a practical form. A build is as much about who I want to be as what I want to defeat.
That would mean less to me if the people around my character were merely there to perform their parts in her story. What caught my attention was how much they could participate in the same world. Their equipment, abilities and allegiances affect what happens. A weapon can pass from an enemy’s hands into mine, and from mine to a companion’s. Other people can fight one another without waiting for me to settle everything. I can assess a situation and intervene in it.
I am not claiming that every villager has a convincingly simulated life. I noticed the repetitive routines early on. What matters more to me is whether people and objects can become part of what I am doing: whether an ally can help, an item can be put to use, or a relationship can matter outside a conversation. These connections give me reasons to pay attention.
Over time, paying attention became a pleasure in its own right. I began to notice patterns in how characters behaved, form expectations and revise them when something unexpected happened. Often I was not trying to improve my character at all; I simply wanted to understand why something had happened. Understanding more of the machinery did not make the world less interesting. It gave me more to notice. I have never needed Skyrim to hide the fact that it is a game; I enjoy getting to know how this particular game works.
Companions are especially important to me. Giving someone better armour, helping them survive a difficult fight and relying on them to deal with an enemy all have a tangible purpose. They make the protective role I enjoy playing worthwhile. I can spend a fight keeping other people alive and still feel that I have contributed. I like being useful without having to be the only useful person present.
There is also continuity to these experiences. When I return to a save, I am picking up a character whose equipment, companions and circumstances have taken shape through earlier decisions. A piece of armour may remind me of where I found it or whom I passed it on to. The world does not preserve everything forever, but enough carries over for my time in it to feel cumulative.
Just as importantly, I can usually set my own pace. I can take another road, return to town, bring help, or decide that a quest can wait. I do not need every problem to admit some ingenious alternative solution. Often, I simply want the ordinary options to remain available once a quest has begun. Accepting an objective need not mean surrendering the rest of the evening to it.
Towns matter as much as the roads between them. I like having somewhere familiar to return to, somewhere to sort through equipment and prepare for another journey. Not every session needs a major battle, a revelation or a completed quest. Sometimes travelling with companions and getting home again is enough. Those quieter stretches are part of what I come back for.
None of this makes Skyrim perfectly consistent, nor does it make every limitation charming. Understanding why an awkward piece of behaviour occurs does not automatically turn it into good design. My affection rests on how often the game’s systems work together to accommodate the way I want to play, rather than on a belief that they never fail.
I recommend Skyrim for the room it gives me to make a character my own and to care about what happens around her. The appeal is not confined to choosing dialogue or pursuing the strongest build. It lies in all the smaller decisions through which a character becomes mine: what she carries, whom she helps, and when she stays or leaves.
After ten years, I do not need another grand reason to go back. There is a character I enjoy being, company I enjoy keeping, and a world I still find worth paying attention to. That is more than enough for another evening in Skyrim.

Having this big world with a legendary soundtrack makes the act of exploring the world to be very very cool. The soundtrack itself is wonderful. I can't tell you how many times I have listened to tracks from this game because I have just listened to this game's soundtrack way too much.

Aside from the exploration and the soundtrack the visuals of this game are timeless. I played this game way after the game was released and everyone was playing it.

Some advice that I can give for playing this are just use the main storyline for the 2 factions as a general roadmap and same can be said for your Dragonborn questline. The main faction quests are not very interesting. It feels more like they were made to get you out there in the world and explore. That being said you should look at the side quests as the main attraction for this game if you are the type to focus on the quests. Just don't go into the Imperial or Stormcloak questlines looking for a good storyline. It just has you going from one enemy outpost to another to kill members of the opposing faction. I did both sides to see if there was a difference and there was pretty much no difference.

Buy this game when it is on sale because Bethesda doesn't deserve the money after coming out with only "Fallout 76" (a side project game) and "Starfield"/"Slopfield" in the past 11 years and Bethesda just isn't the same as it used to be and that is to be expected.

Even with what I said in the previous paragraph I say that this is just one of those classic games that I think everyone should give a chance. For me I come back to this game at least once a year and go around the world while listening to the soundtrack and doing whatever. This game is now like comfort food. This is a must buy when it is on sale. Also this game will give you a greater appreciation for games that have come after like "Elden Ring", "Crimson Desert", "Dying Light 1", "Red Dead Redemption 2", and other open world games, but don't go thinking here I would say Bethesda of today is on the same level as the studios that have made the games I listed here. Bethesda isn't even close to being as good as the studios who made the other games I listed here.

Do you know that quote from Family Guy when Peter says, “There’s one more secret I feel I have to share with you: I did not care for The Godfather”? Well, I have the exact same feeling about Skyrim.

I know this game is beloved by so many people, and I went into it with really high expectations, but in the end, it just didn't click with me. Most of the quests I played felt pretty mid, and nothing in the game really stood out enough for me to fall in love with it.

Maybe part of the reason is that I played Skyrim after playing the Fallout games. After getting used to guns and the faster-paced gameplay in those games, Skyrim felt much slower to me. Maybe that's the reason I couldn't get into it, or maybe it's just not my type of game. Honestly, I don't know.

Even the intro didn't impress me that much. Compared to the intro of Oblivion, Skyrim's opening just didn't feel as cool or memorable to me.

I had really high hopes for Skyrim because of its reputation, but unfortunately, it ended up being a letdown for me. I can understand why so many people love it, but personally, I just didn't find much that stood out.

Maybe I'm missing something, but Skyrim just wasn't for me.

Why can't they just leave a separate branch of the game without these updates? For people who just want to play with their mods in peace without worrying the next patch is gonna wreck everything. Instead they keep breaking a system that works, over and over, for content and updates literally nobody asked for.

And I gotta ask separately, what does Asha Sharma even think about all this? Because it really feels like instead of finally working on TES 6, which everyone's been waiting years for, they're throwing resources at squeezing a bit more cash out of a game that's about to turn fifteen. Since 2011 Skyrim's been released nine times.

Go wild on consoles, there's nothing to fix there and not much to break anyway. All they cared about was bumping the mod limit, and PC players couldn't care less about that, barely anyone even uses that stuff. Just leave the PC version alone already, for Talos' sake.
